approved: Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill 2013

Argued the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill 2013 is a coalition stunt, noting the explanatory memorandum shows it will save only $0.25 million on an underlying cash basis over the forward estimates, or $250,000 over four years.

Argued Labor turned a $50 billion surplus in 2007 into $450 billion of gross debt by 2013, and defended the coalition's push to cut $1 billion in red and green tape, citing the abolition of the carbon and mining taxes.

Blamed six years of Labor mismanagement for leaving taxpayers and future generations facing worse schools, bridges, roads and hospitals, and urged passage of the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill 2013 while rejecting the opposition's amendment.
Introduced remarks on the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill 2013 by previewing the total savings the bill would deliver.
Welcomed the bill ending $900 stimulus cheques that had continued to be sent up to five years after the global financial crisis.

Defended Labor's $95 billion global financial crisis stimulus package, citing Nobel laureate Joseph Stiglitz's estimate that it saved up to 200,000 jobs, and criticised the Abbott government for 50,000 job losses in its first five months, including at Holden and Toyota.

Criticised the tax bonus scheme for sending more than 21,000 payments worth over $18 million to deceased taxpayers, and disputed Labor's stimulus record by citing a claim that households spent just $1 extra of each $900 payment on non-durable goods.

Defended Labor's GFC stimulus package, citing Treasury secretary Ken Henry's evidence that the mining industry shed 15.2 per cent of its workforce and that a similar economy-wide response would have pushed unemployment to 19 per cent, and noted the package included $28.8 billion in direct investment in infrastructure and services.

Recounted his unshown 2009 speech warning that Labor's stimulus plan would lift debt to $200 billion, or $9,500 per Australian, and said more than 21,000 tax bonus cheques have been mailed to dead people since, against a now-projected $667 billion gross debt.

Called for the tax bonus scheme's repeal, pointing to 16,000 payments worth about $40 million sent to people overseas and $18 million paid to deceased recipients, and projected gross debt reaching $667 billion, or two-thirds of $1 trillion, within a decade under Labor's settings.

Defended Labor's stimulus record, citing Australia's 23rd consecutive year of economic growth and more than 960,000 jobs created while 27 million jobs were lost worldwide, and highlighted the $42 billion Nation Building and Jobs Plan that funded over 9,500 school building projects.

Rejected claims of Labor economic success, contrasting the Howard government's average annual growth of 3.6 per cent with 2.5 per cent under the Rudd-Gillard governments, and noted 480,000 tax bonus payments worth more than $400 million had been made since the original 2009 stimulus, warning of peak debt reaching $667 billion.

Illustrated the tax bonus scheme's flaws with a Bundaberg fruit grower, Craig van Rooyen, still receiving stimulus cheques for backpackers long gone, and noted more than 21,000 payments worth over $18 million have gone to deceased people since the scheme began.

Backed repeal of the tax bonus scheme, citing a Treasury estimate that households spent less than 0.2 per cent of their $900 stimulus payment, and warned that mounting debt would reach $667 billion, costing $10 billion a year in interest.

Supported repealing the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Act, saying Labor borrowed $7.7 billion for the $900 stimulus cheques and that over 480,000 payments worth $400 million were made after the global financial crisis had passed.

Supported repealing the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Act, noting the previous government sent out 15,000 additional $900 cheques with borrowed money in the 2012-13 financial year alone, and cited local reactions from Cairns residents on how they spent the original payments.

Argued during debate on the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill that Australia's resilience during the global financial crisis owed more to regional economic strength than Labor's stimulus spending, noted GDP per capita fell by 0.8 per cent in 2008 to 2009, and said the unemployment queue grew by 200,000 people under the Labor government.

Supported the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Repeal Bill to stop further $900 stimulus payments, cited $667 billion in projected government debt as Labor's legacy, and recounted how a Tasmanian gaming venue's takings rose by $75,000 in the week the cheques were paid, calling the scheme wasteful and poorly targeted.

Supported repealing the Tax Bonus for Working Australians scheme, arguing untargeted cash payments have little economic multiplier effect, citing an example where a $1,000 payment mostly bought an imported television, and criticised the schoolkids bonus for not requiring recipients to spend it on their children.

Supported repealing the Tax Bonus for Working Australians Act, noting more than 430,000 cheques worth over $375 million were issued after the year the stimulus was intended for, including 15,000 cheques worth nearly $13 million in the last financial year alone, and cited Labor's forecast $123 billion in deficits heading towards $667 billion in debt.
